items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping decision-making processes and infrastructures. It is also changing how societies narrate risk, responsibility, and the future. Existing scholarship has examined these representations and their ethical implications. Yet it rarely offers comprehensive approaches to analyzing the functions narratives perform in shaping ethical debates. Understanding these functions is crucial for grasping how narratives influence ethical judgment and public discourse about AI. To address this gap, this paper proposes a conceptual framework for examining them. Rather than analyzing narrative content or audience reception, we focus on narrative structure. We ask how these structures shape normative assumptions and guide ethical evaluation. We grounded the analysis in a qualitative integrative review. We developed a typology linking three narrative functions to three waves of ethical concern about AI. The framework offers a heuristic tool for analyzing how ethical discourse around AI is formed, contested, and transformed. More broadly, the paper promotes reflective, context-sensitive approaches to AI governance and public understanding. This is especially important today, as AI’s disruption means that humans no longer shape narratives alone.
items.title: When human narratives meet artificial intelligence: exploring a framework for AI ethics

items.abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of a first‐in‐human (FIH) clinical trial is to gather safety, side effects, and (potential) dosage information, which is to say, information about how an intervention affects and interacts with the human body. Although participants in FIH trials may personally benefit, the primary goal is to obtain participant baseline human safety knowledge or knowledge of intervention efficacy. Some FIH clinical trials carry significant foreseeable risk to participants with little to no foreseeable participant benefit. As the potential risk is high and personal benefit unlikely, there is consensus that participants in risky FIH trials should consent to participate, which entails that children should not be included in a risky FIH trial that could enroll only adults. We take aim at this view and argue that risky FIH trials planned for adults should be open also to including children in some circumstances. Specifically, and focusing primarily on solid organ xenotransplant research, we argue that considerations of generalizability, fair inclusion, differential risk‐benefit, parental authority, and children's interest are ethically salient, and that concerns of exploitation, instrumentalization, and upper‐limits of harm can be effectively addressed.
items.title: The Case for Pediatric Participation in Risky First‐In‐Human Clinical Trials

items.abstract:
Private rights have returned to play a central role in public law. In the last few years alone, courts have invoked private rights to elaborate the elements of Article III standing, interpret the scope of 42 U.S.C. § 1983’s cause of action, articulate the limits of the administrative state, and give meaning to enumerated constitutional rights. But unlike private law—which has confronted a similar fall and rise of private rights with wide-ranging discussion over their meaning—public law has not been subjected to a fulsome debate about what exactly private rights are. Both proponents and critics of the return of a private rights model of public law adjudication share a basic understanding of private rights rooted in William Blackstone’s eighteenthcentury writings. But Blackstone’s view fails to capture the full significance of private rights in the common law. Overemphasizing it muddles the stakes of the return of private rights in public law.

This Article articulates the historical and doctrinal limits of the default Blackstonian view of private rights. Blackstone’s conception of private rights was based on an underlying view of liberty as noninterference that was controversial even when he was writing in the 1760s. Instead, the dominant view of liberty in the common law at the time was the republican view of liberty as independence. That view of liberty supported a distinct republican conception of private rights, which has coexisted in the common law tradition alongside the Blackstonian conception.

After outlining the oft-elided republican conception of private rights and tracing its influence on legal discourse, rhetoric, and case law, this Article illustrates its possible implications for public law doctrine. Recognizing the distinction between these two conceptions of private rights casts new light on Article III standing, damages, Section 1983, and adjudication outside Article III courts. This distinction also provides a corrective to the scholarly debates over private and public rights: Just as it is a mistake to suppose there was a single unified historical conception of private rights, it is also a mistake to dismiss private rights altogether as inherently confused or obfuscatory.
items.title: “Private Rights” in Public Law

items.abstract:
Federalism has long been celebrated for its ability to foster policy innovation, transforming states into “laboratories of democracy.” Yet, federalism discourse has largely neglected Indian tribes, the third sovereign in the American constitutional order. Tribes regularly implement novel policies. However, tribal policy innovation is hindered by uncertainty over whether tribes or states govern Indian country activities.

The most influential framework for determining the scope of tribal versus state regulatory power in Indian country is derived from the Supreme Court’s opinion in California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians—the case that launched Indian gaming. Cabazon held that tribes cannot permit an activity if the surrounding state prohibits it, but they can permit an activity if the surrounding state regulates it. For example, tribes in California can authorize gaming because California regulates it. However, Utah’s gaming ban prevents tribes within its borders from permitting casinos. The distinction between regulatory and prohibitory is often ambiguous; thus, state specificity invites endless litigation that stifles tribal policy experimentation.

To remedy this uncertainty and fully integrate tribes into the federal system, this Article proposes a “Cabazon-plus” paradigm. Under Cabazon-plus, if any state regulates an activity, all tribes would have exclusive regulatory authority over that activity. This paradigm provides the jurisdictional certainty vital for tribal self-determination and policy innovation. Furthermore, this Article argues Cabazon-plus will ignite tribal economies and benefit state economies, validating tribal sovereignty as a feature—not a bug—of a dynamic federal system.
items.title: Tribal Federalism: Expanding the Indian Gaming Paradigm
